html:
From 1788 to 1868 Britain shipped about 160,000 convicts to its Australian colonies as punishment. It was the main way the colonies were peopled in their first decades.

Transportation, sending criminals to a distant colony, had sent convicts to North America until the American War of Independence ended that. Australia replaced it, starting with the First Fleet. Most convicts were young working class men from English and Irish cities, sent for theft. Some were political prisoners: Irish rebels, machine breakers, and the Tolpuddle Martyrs, farm labourers punished for forming a union.

Many convicts were assigned to work for settlers or the government, building roads and buildings. Reoffenders went to harsh penal stations such as Port Arthur in Van Diemen's Land and Norfolk Island. When their terms ended most stayed, and freed convicts and their children made up much of the early population. Opposition in the colonies ended transportation to New South Wales in 1840; the last convict ship reached Western Australia in 1868.
sum: From 1788 to 1868 Britain shipped about 160,000 convicts to its Australian colonies as punishment. It was the main way the colonies were peopled in their first decades.
